Employers need to confirm that the doctor or specialist is registered with the correct body (GMC, GDC or UKPHR) and has no restrictions to practise or ongoing investigations.

Job planning

All consultants in public health should have an annual job plan agreed between the consultant and the employer. The job plan sets out the agreed duties, responsibilities and objectives for the coming year and should include a breakdown of how the consultant’s working time is allocated across their duties and responsibilities. The annual job plan also forms an important part of the submission for the national clinical impact awards, and if employers do not adequately support consultants in job planning, it can prevent medical and dental consultants from applying for the national clinical impact award scheme.

Typically, the working week of a full-time consultant will comprise 10 programmed activities or sessions. The Faculty of Public Health recommends that consultants should be allocated 7.5 sessions per week for public health duties and 2.5 sessions per week for supporting professional activities, with a higher proportion of supporting professional activities for those working part-time. Supporting professional activities include CPD, appraisal and revalidation, teaching and training, research, and other work such as Faculty of Public Health examining or committee work.

See the faculty website for further guidance on job planning.

Pay

Pay scales across the public health system vary between the NHS, civil service, local authorities and higher education institutions. Consultant posts are mobile across the system, therefore, an important consideration for employers will be the ability to recruit and retain this specialist group. Higher education institutions have nationally negotiated higher education pay scales for consultant clinical academic doctors and dentists which take into account market comparability with doctors and dentists working in the NHS. Further information can be obtained from the employing higher education institution or from the Universities and Colleges Employers Association, which represents higher education employers in the relevant annual pay negotiations.

Local authorities should consider the relevant market when deciding the pay, terms and conditions for a role. If market supplements are considered, employers should reference any guidance provided through national negotiating bodies to ensure that equal pay considerations are satisfied. Employers should consider that, where consultants in public health are employed in the NHS, UKHSA or DHSC, they are appointed on either medical and dental terms and conditions for medically qualified consultants or Agenda for Change bands 8d or 9 for consultants from backgrounds other than medicine. Employers will want to consider this when setting pay, terms and conditions to remain competitive in the employment market.

The Public Health Medicine Consultative Committee, a joint committee of the British Medical Association and the Faculty of Public Health, published further advice on employing consultants in public health (PDF, 170KB), including on job evaluation for public health consultant roles that local authorities can consider alongside other technical advice.

Continuity of service

Within local government and the health service, some contractual benefits are normally based on the employee’s length of continuous service, for example, annual leave and enhanced maternity rights. Statutory redundancy entitlements are also based on continuous service, and enhancements above the statutory entitlement are often based on a measure of continuous service. However, although the terms and conditions and ways of measuring continuous service in the health service and local government share some similarities, they are separate and distinct.

Where employees move voluntarily from a health service body to a local authority or the Civil Service and vice versa, there is no obligation on the new employer to recognise service with the previous employer for the purposes of contractual benefits, such as annual leave and for redundancy purposes. Therefore, employees who have built up service and, therefore, associated contractual and redundancy entitlements may be reluctant to move from a health service body to a local authority, and vice versa. This can create a barrier to recruitment and make it difficult for public health specialists to move between public health employers, preventing them from developing experience across the breadth of public health practice.

It is recommended that employers make every effort to recognise past service. In 2015, LGA set out how local authorities can use their current discretionary powers to best effect to recognise past service with NHS or Civil Service bodies where an individual voluntarily takes up a local authority post. This includes supporting continued access to the NHS Pension Scheme with an NHS Pension Direction Order. For guidance on how to make a public health open direction and determination, see the NHS Business Services Authority website, under the section application guidance for a pension direction and/or determination.

LGA published the standards for employers of public health teams, which contains further guidance on enabling:

employers to provide a well-led and supportive professional environment

public health professionals to maintain their professionalism

The Faculty of Public Health expects those invited to interview to meet its standards, including being up to date with their CPD. The Faculty of Public Health also expects applicants to be members of the Faculty of Public Health, either as a fellow of the Faculty of Public Health (FFPH) or as a member of the Faculty of Public Health (MFPH). However, this is not a requirement for appointment, unlike the requirements to hold GMC, GDC or UKPHR specialist registration.

Public health specialists can be medically qualified or from backgrounds other than medicine and may work across the breadth of public health practice in different employers. It is therefore recommended that employers seek parity, using established or equivalent terms and conditions for consultants in public health across public health employers. Mobility across sectors and employers within the public health workforce is critical to:

develop the pipeline of future senior public health leadership

support workforce flexibility

retain a broad base of experience and improve system resilience

Most public health consultant posts are open to all specialist registrants in public health. In the extremely rare circumstances where the employer believes that a post might be restricted to only some registered persons, this should be discussed with the Faculty of Public Health registrar, as the person responsible for professional standards and good public health practice in the workforce. See appendix A for information on the professional requirements relating to the appointment of a consultant in public health.

Designing the consultant role

The Faculty of Public Health provides a template job description and person specification for use in consultant in public health appointments in local authorities and consultant in academic public health positions. Some local authorities may use alternative titles for these positions in line with other job titles in the authority, such as assistant director of public health or head of service. However, a Faculty of Public Health-approved job description and person specification should be used if the post is to have the title ‘consultant in public health’. See the faculty website for job descriptions.

To support national consistency for roles at this level, employers should incorporate the full contents of the Faculty of Public Health’s template into their local job description format. For higher education institutions, this should also reflect the Follett principles. The principles are a set of management guidelines governing the employment of clinical academics who work jointly for the NHS and higher education institutions which can be adapted for other employers. These should be adapted with reference to the appropriate honorary contract and joint working arrangements made with both the employer and the institution holding the honorary contract. NHS Employers and the Universities and Colleges Employers Association have produced guidance on the Follett principles for higher education institutions and NHS provider organisations. This also provides a useful framework for other organisations entering into joint working or honorary contract arrangements.

Employers should include the qualification and registration requirements in the job description and on the application form, and candidates, if shortlisted, should be asked to bring the relevant proof to the interview.

Joint appointments

Some local authorities use joint appointments or secondment arrangements for consultants in public health with integrated care boards (ICBs), NHS trusts, NHS foundation trusts or other local authorities as part of joint or integrated working arrangements (for examples, see appendix B). These arrangements may have specific statutory requirements for appointment and employment processes, which should be considered when designing such roles.

When designing a joint role, employers should give practical arrangements the same attention as the job design. These arrangements support effective recruitment and induction and should be agreed between employing organisations through a memorandum of understanding or service level agreement. Considerations should include:

office working locations

allowance for travel time and mileage between workplaces

meeting attendance requirements

time management

IT access

line management and professional lines of accountability

interactions with wider system partners

deputising arrangements and team support across employing organisations

Using interim or locum consultant appointments

Where it is not possible to make a permanent appointment (for example, the appointment is to cover a period of parental leave or long-term illness), employers may choose to use an interim, fixed-term appointment, or use a locum through an agency for up to 6 months. However, this is not recommended as a long-term solution to a vacancy.

When making temporary appointments, employers should ensure that the interim or locum consultant meets the required standard for the role and is assessed by an appointments committee that includes at least 2 public health professionals. This is to prevent issues such as ‘fitness to practise’ concerns or failure to maintain good public health practice. These issues disproportionately occur when locum and interim arrangements are used without applying the same process as substantive posts. The recruiting manager (usually the director of public health) and the HR department should work together to ensure:

the person holds the required specialist registration (set out in the standard Faculty of Public Health person specification)

The role of the Faculty of Public Health and faculty adviser in the appointment process is to:

provide advice to the employer on the consultant job description, advert and person specification and to give a definitive opinion as to whether they fulfil the technical and professional elements required to protect and improve health and provide advice on health services

provide a list of representatives of the Faculty of Public Health for the employer to approach to act as an assessor to sit on the AAC for every consultant appointment to assess and advise on the necessary technical and professional skills, qualifications and professional registration issues

As part of its appointment procedures, the Faculty of Public Health requires that the faculty assessor is involved in the shortlisting of candidates to ensure that they meet the professional qualifications and requirements for a consultant in public health ahead of interview. The faculty assessors will act as the link with the Faculty of Public Health who will carry out validation checks on whether the applicants meet the professional qualifications and requirements to fulfil the role. This usually takes less than one working day to carry out.

Regional faculty advisers can assist by:

identifying the appropriate type of assessor for the role being appointed, for example, where their background or experience aligns with the role being recruited to

confirming to the local authority or higher education institution through validation checks whether their preferred candidate has the necessary specialist public health skills to undertake the role

confirming whether specialist registrars are within 6 months of completing their training and due to receive their certificate of completion of training, and are therefore eligible to be shortlisted

providing evidence to the employer before interviews take place if, following validation checks, a candidate does not have the specialist public health qualifications, skills and registration needed to undertake the role

The role of the employer associations in appointing a consultant in public health

The Local Government Association (LGA) and the Universities and Colleges Employers Association provide sector-specific advice on issues relating to recruitment processes and pay, terms and conditions of employment.

Appendix A: essential professional requirements for consultants in public health

Professional regulation

Consultants in public health from backgrounds other than medicine are registered with the UKPHR.

Medical and dental public health consultants are regulated by GMC and GDC.

The following routes of specialist training and assessment provide assurance of competence:

undertaking Faculty of Public Health specialty training and obtaining a certificate of completion of training for registrants from backgrounds other than medicine, and medical and dental backgrounds

demonstrating competence by submitting a retrospective portfolio that is assessed and approved by the Faculty of Public Health (for admission to the GMC specialist register) or the UKPHR (for admission to the UKPHR register)

Any appointment to a consultant in public health or consultant in academic public health post in line with Faculty of Public Health appointment procedures must be of an individual who is either:

on the GMC full and specialist register with a licence to practise in:

public health medicine

a specialty other than public health and able to demonstrate equivalent training or appropriate experience of public health practice, for example, through the GMC portfolio route

on the GDC specialist list in:

dental public health

a specialty other than dental public health and able to demonstrate equivalent training or appropriate experience of public health practice, for example, through the GMC portfolio route

on the UKPHR for public health specialists

a public health specialty registrar who is currently on the UK public health training programme and not yet on the GMC, GDC or UKPHR specialist register, and who can provide verifiable signed documentary evidence that they are within 6 months of gaining entry to a register at the date of interview

Note that applicants going through the portfolio registration routes (GMC or UKPHR) are not eligible to be shortlisted for interview until they are included on the register. The 6-month rule does not apply to these portfolio route applicants.

Revalidation

Revalidation is the process by which UKPHR and GMC public health registrants demonstrate that they have met their required professional standards, including:

CPD

quality improvement activity

annual professional appraisal

reflective practice

Employers should note that, for GMC registrants, revalidation is a requirement to maintain their licence to practise. Registrants are required to maintain a link to:

a designated body (a UK healthcare organisation approved by the GMC to oversee the revalidation and clinical governance of licensed doctors)

a responsible officer (a senior doctor appointed by a designated body to oversee the professional conduct, annual appraisal and revalidation of its medical staff)

Licensed doctors should use the GMC connection tool to find out their revalidation connection type.

Responsible officers in Great Britain are responsible for revalidation recommendations to GMC in respect of individual doctors.

Both UKPHR and GMC publish guidance and resources on the revalidation process. While the requirements are broadly similar, the approaches to revalidation vary slightly between UKPHR and GMC, and employers should consult the relevant regulator’s guidance on revalidation.

DHSC acts as the designated body for revalidation for:

GMC registrants, where appropriate, for all doctors for whom it is the employing organisation
